To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
sleep duration varies by demographic factors and longer sleep is associated with more healthy weight related behaviors and a lower risk of central obesity.

Longer sleep is associated, longitudinally, with more healthy weight related behaviors (e.g. having breakfast, eating healthy snacks) and less unhealthy weight related behaviors (sugar sweetened beverage intake and total screen time) among children aged 6-17 years in China.

1) sleep duration varied across demographic factors; 2) longer sleep was associated with healthier weight-related behaviors and lower central adiposity risk; 3) sleep duration was associated with weight-related behaviors in both cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses, and with central obesity in longitudinal analysis; 4) longer sleep was longitudinally observed in younger, and primary school children and those with college-educated parents.
